utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, these are two decisions, No. 16 and No. 17, which appeared 7 in the Banja Luka Gazette. They are decisions No. 16 of 8 22nd May 1992 and it relates to apartments and tenancies within 9 opstina Prijedor. The second document, article No. 17, is dated 10 26th May 1992 and it is a conclusion of the regional Crisis 11 Staff of the Autonomous Region Krajina. It outlines a number of things in relation to the 13 recommendation of judges and prosecutors for the basic courts. 14 It then outlines that leading posts in the social and public 15 organisations can be occupied only by the most professional 16 cadre that is absolutely loyal to the Serb people in the Serb 17 Republic Bosnia and Herzegovina. It then outlines about 18 management boards in stock companies, the control of people in 19 the communes, a committee to be formed for negotiations with 20 members of other nationalities, an agency that would work on the 21 problem of population immigration and a paragraph in relation to 22 sales tax -- two paragraphs actually in relation to sales tax.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Reid, what is the Banja Luka Gazette?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Banja Luka Gazette is the official organ, if I can put it 25 that way, of the Autonomous Region Krajina and it is usually for 26 decisions, conclusions, all the official communications of the 27 regional Crisis -- among other bodies, the regional Crisis Staff 28 for the Autonomous Region of Krajina. 1 MR. TIEGER: Your Honour, I wish to tender these documents, but I should indicate (and that is why I made the point about identification) that these are English translations of portions of Exhibit 145. I did not know if the Court wanted to have them marked accordingly as a portion of 145 or just proceed chronologically. I am not sure there is a perfect solution, but I wanted to leave that to the Court. 8 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: I do not know. I do not have a preference. 145, we do not have it as an A or B. It is just 145. Do you know, Mr. Bos? 11 MR. TIEGER: No, it is just one -- it is a bundle of papers marked as one exhibit and not ---- 13 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: This would be then the English translation of portions of decisions in there? 15 MR. TIEGER: Yes. If I remember correctly, there are English translations which comprise part of Exhibit 145 already. 17 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: I do not know. Why do we not leave it as it is? This way we will know that they are English translations of the decisions 16 and 17. I gather 16 and 17, the Serbo-Croat, are in 145? 21 THE WITNESS: Cyrillic. 22 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: Cyrillic? 23 THE WITNESS: Yes, your Honour, yes. It is in Cyrillic. The entire Gazette that we have is in Cyrillic. There are a number of individual English translations of those decisions. 26 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: Let us leave it the way it is then. It will be 367A and B and we understand what it is, only because we do not have 145 before us and we will have to look at that and see how it might relate. Just leave it this way. Is there any objection to 367A and B? 3 MR. KAY: No, your Honour. 4 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: They will be admitted. 5 MR. TIEGER: Mr. Reid, are you familiar with two witnesses who testified in this case, Hakija Elezovic and Samir Hodzic? 7 A. Yes, I am. 8 Q. Do you know whether or not they lived in the same country at the time they gave their initial statements? 10 A. No, they did not. They lived on separate continents. 11 Q. To your knowledge, did they continue to live on separate continents thereafter as well? 13 A. No, they did not. 14 Q. Do you know the distance from Sisak to Kozarac? 15 JUDGE STEPHEN: I am sorry. I do not know if I followed that last answer. They no longer live in separate continents? 17 A. They live in the same area currently, your Honour. 18 Q. You mean the same area as they previously did? 19 A. No, no, one -- they live together now. 20 JUDGE STEPHEN: Yes, thank you. 21 THE WITNESS: Yes, the distance from Sisak to Kozarac is approximately 70 kilometres as the crow flies. It would probably be at the very, very most an hour and a half, two hour, drive between the two locations. 25 MR. TIEGER: Did you have an opportunity to examine the unredacted traffic police rosters which were obtained during the course of the video link testimony? 28 A. Yes, I did. I have not examined the entire roster, but I have examined a couple of pages of it. 2 Q. In examining portions of that roster of traffic policemen, did you find the names of any persons who were reported to have been involved in the round-up or selection of Muslims to go to camps or any other aspect of the ethnic cleansing? 6 A. Yes. Can I refer to the document that I have? 7 Q. Yes. 8 A. The document that I was given, on the very first page, 16th June 1992, there are two names there, at No. 706 the Kozarac checkpoint, Zeljko Maric. Statements have been taken from at least three witnesses that implicate that person in the roundup of people fleeing from Kozarac. The other person that is on this roster is marked No. 3 under the heading "slobodni" which, I believe, means "day off" or "rest day". It is No. 3, Bosko Grabez. We have a number of statements from witnesses who were taken from the Omarska camp to Manjaca camp on 6th August 1992 where that person travelled on one of the buses as a guard on the bus. There are further statements from witnesses that say that that person was involved in the murder of a person at the front of Manjaca camp on the night of 6th August/morning of 7th August, 1992. 23 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: Which Exhibit is that? Do you have an Exhibit number on that roster? 25 MR. TIEGER: 66C, your Honour. 26 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: I missed it, sorry. 27 MR. TIEGER: D66C, I should add. 28 JUDGE STEPHEN: I am afraid I missed the second name, Grabez? 1 THE WITNESS: Grabez, your Honour, yes, spelt G-R-A-B-E-Z. 2 JUDGE STEPHEN: Thank you. 3 MR. KAY: I think there is an error on the transcript which had it down as Bosko Dragicevic who is someone else entirely. 5 MR. TIEGER: Let me have a moment, your Honour. I apologise, your Honour, I am sorry. Your Honour, may I have these marked as 368A through D? Mr. Reid, are these articles from Kosarksi Vjesnik in which there are photographs depicting persons in various uniforms at various times? 11 A. Yes, that is correct, yes. 12 MR. TIEGER: Your Honour, I am going to tender those Exhibits. They really speak for themselves and also I will be submitting some colour photographs of uniforms as well in response to the Court's request. 16 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: Is there any objection? 17 MR. KAY: No objection, your Honour. 18 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: Exhibit 368A and B will be admitted. 19 MR. TIEGER: Those will be A through D, your Honour. 20 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: 368A through D then are admitted. 21 MR. TIEGER: I think this can be submitted as simply Exhibit 369. The Defence may want to take a look at that. They are just photographs of various uniforms. Mr. Reid, in 369 do you see any photographs showing an SMB uniform? 26 A. Yes, in the first five photographs they are SMB uniforms and the one on top is the winter uniform. 28 Q. Can we have one of those placed on the overhead projector, please? 2 A. This is the winter uniform. 3 MR. TIEGER: It looks like it is not going to happen, your Honour. 4 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: However you want to handle it; if you wish, you can just hand them up to the Bench and we will take a look at them. 7 MR. TIEGER: Mr. Reid, does 369 show the SMB uniform and various camouflage uniforms? 9 A. Yes, the last two photographs in the pile are the camouflage uniforms of the former JNA. 11 Q. The previous Exhibit, did the photographs in those Exhibits or that Exhibit also depict soldiers in both SMB and camouflage uniforms? 14 A. Yes. There is one there that I noticed where there is a unit being inspected and there were soldiers within that unit wearing civilian clothes as well. 17 MR. TIEGER: I imagine the Court will have time to review that at its leisure. 19 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: It is working, if you want to show us. 20 THE WITNESS: This is the winter uniform of the JNA. 21 MR. TIEGER: Does "SMB" refer to the particular style of uniform or to the colour? 23 A. No, I think it is the colour. It is the particular colour that they refer to. They never say an olive green or a green or a black or a grey. It is always an SMB uniform and it always refers to the JNA uniform. 27 Q. I understand there are also a couple of photographs showing one or another type of camouflage uniform? 1 A. Yes, there are. 2 JUDGE STEPHEN: The witness mentioned that one photograph was the winter uniform. This is the first I have heard of a winter uniform. Is that a winter SMB or just ---- 5 A. Yes, that is what I believe, your Honour. 6 Q. As distinct from a summer SMB? 7 A. Yes, your Honour. The summer is, I believe, something like this photograph here and, additionally, this photograph here. 9 JUDGE VOHRAH: That is a different colour. How do you differentiate this uniform from the previous ones? 11 A. I am sorry, your Honour? 12 Q. How do you differentiate this uniform from the previous one? 13 A. This is the previous uniform of the JNA. This is -- I believe that this would be like equivalent to a dress uniform or a full uniform, if you like. This -- I believe this type of uniform is the battle uniform or one that would be used out in the field or around the barracks. 18 Q. The colours are different? 19 A. Yes, sir, but they are still described by witnesses as "SMB". 20 JUDGE VOHRAH: Thank you. 21 THE WITNESS: The camouflage uniforms, and the ..... 22 MR. TIEGER: Was that tendered, your Honour? 23 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: It has not been admitted, I do not think, 369. Is there any objection? 25 MR. KAY: No objection. 26 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: That will be admitted. 27 MR. TIEGER: Mr. Reid, did you review information or have access to information which would indicate whether or not any prisoners who were held in the large hangar building of the Omarska camp were held in portions of the ground floor located to the left of the entrance as one would enter? 4 A. Yes, I do not believe that there were prisoners held in those rooms. The statements that I have looked at, which is every statement that has been taken, no witness has actually said they have been held in that -- in any of those rooms. On the inspection that we did of the large hangar in February and March of this year, it appeared as though a lot of those rooms were where they stored tools, machinery and things like that and they were still basically intact from when it was no longer used as a mine but as a camp. 13 Q. Did the information indicate whether or not any prisoners were held between the area of the entrance and the stairway room? 15 A. Again, there is a large room that has -- there was -- when you go into that room which is pretty much in the middle of that area you are describing, there was a large board with all the names of the workers that either worked in the hangar or the entire mine, I am not sure. That was also an area that housed all the tools and different machines, lathes and things like that, and it appeared as though it had not been used as a room when Omarska was a camp. There were, in fact, people working in that when we were doing our inspection. 24 MR. TIEGER: That is all I have, your Honour, thank you. 25 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: Cross-examination, Mr. Kay?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 27 MR. KAY: Thank you, your Honour. 28 Q. Just a few questions on the last matters you raised, Mr. Reid. You are referring, presumably, to your observations during your visit of February 1996 ---- 3 A. Yes, that is correct. 4 Q. --- which was obviously some considerable period of time since the closure of Omarska as a detention camp? 6 A. Yes, it was closed somewhere around 21st/22nd August 1992. There are a lot of things there though that appeared to be that people had just up and left. There is an area upstairs, the internal stairway, the offices above in that area, there were still desk calendars within the last week of May 1992. There were documents just spread out over desks and it appeared as though that area had not been used either. So it was consistent that there had not really been anybody up in that area as well. 14 Q. Perhaps people may not have been held in those rooms for any significant period, but that is not to say that for periods of time people may have been put in those rooms, perhaps not as permanent places of detention, but they may have been put in there for whatever reason? 19 A. That is correct, yes. 20 Q. The same goes for the ground floor as well? 21 A. Yes, that is correct. 22 Q. It does seem that on occasions the hangar building has been used by various organisations or people since that period of August 1992? 25 A. That is correct. When I was there in February/March, there was a clear line of demarkation, if you like. The bottom level and the internal stairway and the rooms above the internal stairway were being used by the Omarska mine ---- 1 Q. Yes. 2 A. --- and the area from the external stairway that led up to the first floor was being used by the army of Republika Srpska. 4 Q. They, in fact, were using the hangar building, as we are familiar with it in this courtroom, as an ammunition store? 6 A. I believe that is what it may be now. There was ammunition there. 8 Q. Yes. 9 A. But the ammunition store, no, was in the administration building, in the room that has become known as "Mujo's room". That was where the ammunition store was. 12 Q. When you went there in February, were there vast boxes full of weapons or ---- 14 A. In Mujo's room there was, yes, which is in the administration building or the restaurant building. 16 Q. So it seems that there has been certainly people entering this particular camp and using it for other purposes since the days of August 1992? 19 A. Yes, that is correct. 20 Q. I would like to ask you now a couple of other questions about other matters. I think I will start with the photo procedures. You have referred to an investigator, presumably, from the Prosecution team and a separate investigator, as a law enforcement officer, who undertook the identification procedures in relation to the four witnesses who claimed not to have known Dusko Tadic before the conflict? 27 A. Yes, that is correct. 28 Q. First of all, the name of the person from the Office of the Prosecutor or the Prosecution team, who was that? 2 A. It is Mr. Thomas Ackheim. 3 Q. The name of the other person who was a law enforcement officer? 4 A. Is Mr. Ron Safer. 5 Q. Spelt? 6 A. S-A-F-E-R. 7 Q. Were there other law enforcement officers or investigators from the Prosecution used in relation to these procedures? 9 A. Only from the Office of the Prosecutor. There was no other outside law enforcement body used to show the photo spreads. That was the only photospread. 12 Q. We heard evidence from a man called Jos Paepen ---- 13 A. Yes. 14 Q. --- who was involved in one identification process. It seemed to have been his only contact with this particular area. Was he an outside law enforcement officer or did he work for the Office of the Prosecutor? 18 A. No, he worked for the Office of the Prosecutor. He was an investigator or was at that time an investigator with the Office of the Prosecutor. 21 Q. How many such officers are we concerned with? 22 A. The other officer that showed photospreads was Mr. Grant McIntosh who is the other investigator on the team. 24 Q. When these identification procedures were carried out -- we are essentially considering the four that you have given evidence about ---- 27 A. Yes. 28 Q. --- were notes taken at the time of the procedures that were followed? 2 A. I believe that Mr. Safer made notes and Mr. Ackheim, no, he did not. 4 Q. When the identification procedures were carried out, was there any filming of how they were gone about? 6 A. No. 7 Q. Was there any recording of the length of time for which the witness was considering the pages of the photospread? 9 A. No. 10 Q. At what stage during the contact with the witness was the identification book used to enable the procedure to take place? 12 A. Can I refer to my notes? 13 Q. Of course. 14 A. Thank you. In relation to three of the witnesses, a statement was obtained and then the photo book was shown to them sometime after. In relation to the fourth witness, the photo book was shown during the interview of that witness. 18 Q. Are you able to help us with the stage of the interview at which the book was shown? 20 A. I cannot say positively, but I believe that in relation to the witness that was shown the photo book during the interview it was at the end of the interview, the conclusion. 23 Q. The names of the four witnesses we are concerned with here, if you can perhaps give them to us now so that we have them in our minds? 26 A. Sure. The first witness that I speak of is Kasim Mesic, the second one is Sejad Halvadzic, the third one is Senad Muslimovic and the fourth one is Zemka Sahbaz. 1 Q. Of those the one handled by the independent law enforcement officer was which? 3 A. Mr. Muslimovic. 4 Q. Did the officers of the investigation section of the Prosecution team have any pre-written form of words that they had to use in relation to these procedures? Is there a document that set out the precise wording for them to use and the procedures to be followed? 9 A. No, there is not. It is an experience thing. For instance, if I was to show a photo book I really would not need anything written down. It is the same as a record of interview, a handwritten statement, anything like that. I have done it so often. It is an experience thing that you can just go through it. 15 Q. You are familiar, it seems, with procedures that are used in different parts of the world. You told us about the six to eight photographs that may be used by many different jurisdictions as generally the normal spread? 19 A. Yes. 20 Q. Other jurisdictions have procedures that are set out, pro forma documents, that investigating officers use and follow down the page each instruction which is signed? 23 A. Yes. Each individual police force (and the police force I come from) has a set of guidelines, and they are guidelines. You are taught them from the day you join the police until the day you retire, but on occasions the guidelines do vary depending on the witness. For instance, the guidelines for a lineup, they say that the witness should go across, in a physical lineup, a live lineup, the witness should go across to the accused person and touch that person on the shoulder. Some witnesses, particularly sexual assault victims, cannot do that, so they -- so you have to vary the guidelines. It just -- it depends on each individual witness how you do it. 7 Q. So in relation to the procedures we are concerned with for these four witnesses, there was no protocol that was written out that established the guidelines to be used by those two officers? 10 A. No. With Mr. Safer, I am sorry, there were, there were written guidelines for him to follow, and they were sent to him with the photo book as to how to run through it, and that was the sole purpose of Mr. Safer seeing Mr. Muslimovic, was to show him the photo book. 15 Q. What did the guides lines say? 16 A. Basically what I have outlined. If I could refer to another document? 18 Q. Yes, of course. Is this a letter to him? 19 A. No, no, it is not a letter. It is a conversation that I had with him, but he followed it basically to the letter of the law. It is basically what I have outlined in my evidence earlier, that he asked him to look through the book to see if he recognised anyone. I also asked him that if he did recognise anybody, to indicate how he knew that person. Mr. Safer said that, and this is where it varies, the guidelines vary, it appeared quite openly to Mr. Safer that Mr. Muslimovic knew there was a trial going on, so he varied the guidelines that we had given him in that case. He also told him, and we did not tell Mr. Safer whether Mr. Tadic was in the book at all, and then how to go through, handing the book, let him go through it and not to let him spend a lot of time looking at it, and I mean a lot of time to me is to a witness who is perhaps an eyewitness 10 minutes is a long time, from experience. Normally, a person can identify a person fairly quickly, from experience, and that was what -- the guidelines that we set for him. I asked him to have him sign and date any photograph that he identified. 9 Q. So the period of time that seems to have been applied by your investigation team is about 10 minutes for the photo book, is it? 12 A. No, no, that is my own guideline. I would never or very, very rarely let a witness go even that long looking at a photo book. I think, having spoken to Mr. Ackheim, the entire procedure with the three witnesses that he showed from the time that he handed the witness the book to when they flick through it, looked at each of the photographs, identified the photograph, signed and dated it was somewhere in the vicinity of three minutes. That was an average. 20 Q. The witness Muslimovic who was aware of the trial that was going on, he was obviously aware that it was the trial of Dusko Tadic? 22 A. Yes. 23 Q. At what stage then was he put through this procedure? 24 A. His photo board was on 9th May, yes, 9th May, 1996. 25 Q. So after the opening of the case, the trial starting on 7th May? 26 A. Yes. He was interviewed in March, I think, of 1996 -- yes, March 1996 he was interviewed. 28 Q. The country that he was living in? 1 A. He is still living there, so I prefer not to. 2 Q. Which one is that? 3 A. [redacted]. 4 Q. The other three witnesses that were dealt with by the investigator, were they shown the photo book before the trial had started or after the trial had started? Perhaps you can give us the dates for each of those witnesses? 8 A. Yes, Mr. Mesic was shown the photo book on 12th June 1996, Mr. Halvadzic was shown the photo book on 14th June 1996, and Mrs. Sahbaz was shown the book on 31st May 1996. In relation to Mr. Mesic and Mr. Halvadzic, they were shown the book when they were actually here in The Hague. 13 Q. Presumably, when they were shown the book in The Hague, they knew why they had come to The Hague, whose trial it was? 15 A. Yes. 16 Q. It was not a secret? 17 A. No. 18 Q. No. Mr. Sahbaz? 19 A. Mrs. Sahbaz. 20 Q. Mrs. Sahbaz, sorry. She was shown the photo book on 31st May 1996? 22 A. Yes. 23 Q. When had she given her statement? 24 A. She gave her statement on 31st May 1996 as well. We had only just found her at that particular time and she was interviewed immediately. 27 Q. So that was all done at the same time? 28 A. Yes. 1 Q. Draguna Jaskic, is there any indication that she has a connection or association with any of the other witnesses in the case of Mr. Tadic? 4 A. She is the sister -- in relation to these identification witnesses? 6 Q. Yes. 7 A. She lived in the same village, I believe, or in the close proximity to Mrs. Sahbaz, but with the other witnesses, no, I do not believe so. 10 Q. That is Mrs. Sahbaz who did the identification on 31st May ---- 11 A. Yes, I am sorry. 12 Q. --- 1996. 13 A. I thought you were talking about the four identification witnesses. Mrs. Sahbaz would be the only one that she would have any knowledge of, I believe. 16 Q. She may have connections with other witnesses, but of this group of four ---- 18 A. Yes. 19 Q. --- it is the case that it is Mrs. Sahbaz with whom she also has a connection? 21 A. Yes, and I do not know what the connection is today. I know that they lived in the same village or they lived in either Sivci or Jaskici which are in close proximity to each other, but that is basically it. 25 Q. Could one be the sister of the other or sister-in-law? 26 A. No, I do not believe she is the sister-in-law. The sister of Draguna Jaskic is Subha Mujic. 28 Q. Yes, there is one other matter. We have produced the interviews of Mr. Tadic for May and December ---- 2 A. Yes. 3 Q. --- of last year. I am just checking really that they are a complete set because there was a defect in the camera? 5 A. Yes, on the first interview in May the main camera malfunctioned but we had a backup camera, and I think you will find that as tape 5A, I believe. That is complete -- I have checked -- and the interview is complete. 9 Q. The copies their Lordships have been given is a complete transcript? 11 A. Yes, of the entire ---- 12 Q. Without missing pages? 13 A. Yes. 14 Q. Just one other matter as it occurs to me: Witness L, was he taken out to Trnopolje to identify places or sites? 16 A. Yes. 17 Q. Who took him out to the opstina Prijedor region? 18 A. I did, among other people. 19 Q. Was that part of a Prosecution visit to the area? 20 A. No. I took him out. It was arranged specifically to take him to the area and I did that, I believe, on 2nd October of this year. 23 Q. Of this year? 24 A. Yes. 25 Q. I am actually thinking of slightly before the time that we have had the revelation of the issues. 27 A. No. 28 Q. Was he taken out before the trial started or before he gave evidence? 2 A. No, no, not at all. 3 Q. You have been aware of his movements, have you, since he was given to you by the Bosnian police? 5 A. Yes. 6 Q. Thank you. That satisfies me. There has been discussion, as you are aware, between the Defence on the number of witnesses in particular countries and I believe you have talked to Mr. Wladimiroff about this? 10 A. Yes. 11 Q. I am wondering whether the list has been prepared to advise us of the geographic distribution in relation to witnesses? 13 A. Yes, I can tell you the number of witnesses from each of the countries. 15 Q. Yes. 16 A. If that is what you are looking for. I can tell you a breakdown of those witnesses and I have only included fact witnesses, not policy or expert witnesses. [redacted]

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [redacted]. I might add that they are the countries where the people were interviewed and statements were taken from them. They do not necessarily live in those countries now. 27 Q. At this particular time would they have been interviewed in the countries in which they were living at that time? 1 A. Yes. That is the breakdown I have just given you. 2 Q. Yes. Thank you. That is all I ask. 3 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 5 Q. First, your Honour, before I begin can I ask for a redaction at 15.05.26. Mr. Reid, just one matter. You were asked about Draguna Jaskic and Mrs. Sahbaz? 9 A. Yes. 10 Q. You indicated you thought they were from the same place, that is Jaskici or Sivci? 12 A. Yes, in 1992. 13 Q. Yes. Do you know whether or not they were living in the same country thereafter? 15 A. No, they do not live in the same country now. 16 MR. TIEGER: Thank you. That is all. 17 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: Do you have any objection to that redaction? 18 MR. KAY: No, your Honour. 19 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: That will be granted. Do you have additional questions, Mr. Kay? 21 MR. KAY: No thank you, your Honour. 22 JUDGE STEPHEN: A couple of questions, Mr. Reid. The first one was looking across the Court at the model of Omarska there, the large apparently two-storey building at the far end of the hangar we seem to have heard nothing at all about in evidence. Was it entirely separate from the longitudinal part of the hangar? 28 A. There is one door that connects the two buildings and there is no information from any witness that I have seen that that was ever used. 3 Q. Thank you. The other thing I wanted to ask was what you have told us about the procedure with the photospread is entirely what you have been informed by the two different officers who conducted it? You were not present at any of these photospread examinations, were you? 8 A. No, that is correct, sir. 9 JUDGE STEPHEN: Thank you. 10 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: How many different officers conducted it? One who was an independent law enforcement officer and then who else? 13 A. With the four identification witnesses there were only two people involved. One is Mr. Ackheim who showed three witnesses and the other is Mr. Safer who showed Mr. Muslimovic. 16 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: Mr. Tieger, do you have additional questions? 17 MR. TIEGER: One moment, your Honour. No, your Honour. 18 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: Mr. Tieger did you have additional questions? 19 MR. TIEGER: No thank you, your Honour. 20 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: Mr. Kay? 21 MR. KAY: No thank you, your Honour. 22 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: Mr. Reid is permanently excused, I presume? 23 MR. KAY: Yes. 24 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: Thank you for coming. You are excused from coming. 26 THE WITNESS: Thank you, your Honour. (The witness withdrew). 28 JUDGE STEPHEN: Mr. Tieger, you have been good enough to give us Exhibit 366A and B each of which is very lengthy. This is really to help in view of the 6,000 plus pages of transcript that we already have. Will you be drawing our attention to particular passages in the final address of these or are we expected to examine them and compare them with the evidence? What is your intention in giving them to us now? 7 MR. TIEGER: Your Honour, you may be sure that we will be drawing the Court's attention to particular portions of that document. You may recall that that was done during cross-examination as well, and we will give the Court as much guidance as possible in utilizing the evidence which has been presented in a most efficient form. 13 JUDGE STEPHEN: We will look forward to that with interest. Thank you. 15 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: Mr. Tieger, would you call your next witness or Mr. Keegan? 17 MR. KEEGAN: I apologise for this late notice to the Court and also to the Defence. Your Honour, I was literally just informed by the witness who is a German police officer that he requests facial distortion during his testimony. 21 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: We, you need to talk with opposing counsel about that and we will stand in recess for five minutes and see if it can be agreed upon. 24 MR. KEEGAN: Thank you, your Honour. 25 3.15 p.m. (The Court adjourned for a short time). 27 3.20 p.m. 28 MR. TIEGER: Your Honour, for the record I should indicate that during the recess we requested and were granted without objection a redaction from 15.11.48 to 15.12.46. 3 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: That has been granted. 4 MR. KAY: Yes. 5 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: Mr. Keegan, would you call the next witness. 6 MR. KEEGAN: Thank you, your Honour. I call Officer Huebel to the stand, please. 8 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: There is no objection to facial distortion? 9 MR. KAY: No, your Honour. ALFRED HUEBEL, called. 11 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: Sir, would you please take the oath that is being handed to you. 13 THE WITNESS [In translation]: I solemnly declare that I shall tell the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth. 15 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: Fine. Thank you. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 17 MR. KEEGAN: Sir, would you please state your full name? 18 A. Alfred Huebel is my name. 19 Q. What position do you currently hold, sir? 20 A. I am Chief Investigator in Mecklenheim. 21 Q. How long have you held that position? 22 A. I have been with the federal investigation there since 1980. 23 Q. Sir, on 11 and 12 October of 1994 did you conduct an interview of Dusko Tadic? 25 A. With my colleague Officer Balante and myself on that date, we did question Mr. Tadic in Munich in the Stadelheim facility. 27 Q. Do you see the man that you interviewed on that day here in this courtroom? 1 A. Yes, I see Mr. Tadic on my left, here in the middle between the other two gentlemen. 3 Q. OK. I need you, if you would please, to point at him and if you could just describe what he is wearing? 5 A. Yes, Mr. Tadic is wearing a grey suit. He is wearing a blue shirt and a dark tie. 7 Q. Your Honour, if the record could reflect that the witness identified the accused? 9 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: Yes, the record will so reflect. 10 MR. KEEGAN: Could Prosecution Exhibit 321A be given to the witness, please? (Handed). Sir, if you could look at the document that has been handed to you and tell me if you recognise it, please? 13 A. This document here before me is the record of the interview that was carried out by myself and by my colleague in the prison facility in Munich at the time. 16 Q. Sir, if I could ask you to turn to page 18 of that document, it is marked "18" in the bottom right-hand corner of your document. If page 11 could be placed on the Elmo, please, of the English version. Thank you. Sir, if you look at that page 18 in that record of interview. You asked the accused about a document identified as Exhibit 1.12.87 which had been seized from the apartment in Munich where the accused was staying. That document refers to the issuance of an automatic weapon and 300 rounds of ammunition to the accused. When you were referring to that document and your questions to the accused, did you show that document to the accused? 27 A. We did show that document to Mr. Tadic. He did have an opportunity to see it and become acquainted with it. 1 Q. Did you follow that practice for each of the documents which are referred to in the questions in this record of interview? 3 A. Now the Exhibits which are referred to in this document were all produced to Mr. Tadic. 5 Q. Is that a requirement of the operating procedures for the German police authorities? 7 A. That is a procedure that is followed by the German police in such cases. 9 Q. If Exhibit 148 could be shown to the witness, please, Prosecution Exhibit 148. The plastic sleeve must also be shown to the witness. Sir, do you recognise that Exhibit? 12 A. Now on the plastic cover there is a sticker that we put on exhibits. It is my colleague that signed it here. The Exhibit I have here was produced to Mr. Tadic at the time. 15 Q. Thank you. Nothing further, your Honour. 16 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: Mr. Kay, cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 18 Q. If you would like to look at the first page of the questioning of the accused, which is page 3 in the bottom right-hand corner ---- 21 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: This is 321A, is it or 321 I guess? 22 MR. KAY: 321. 23 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: In his language. OK, thank you. 24 MR. KAY: It is headed about "About the Individual". I think it is page 2 of the German document. Can you see that, Officer? 26 A. I have page 2 open here, yes. 27 Q. It states as a comment there that Mr. Tadic was given an opportunity to acquaint himself with the second letter he sent from prison dated 6th March 1994, and agreed to those handwritten 10 pages being included as attachment one. It says that they are included as a seven-page translation by the interpreter Mr. Kertes. Do you see that? 5 A. Yes, I do see it. 6 Q. That specifically refers to a document that was produced to Mr. Tadic during the interview, does it not? 8 A. This was something that had been drafted by Mr. Tadic and that was annexed to the record. 10 Q. But it says here he was given an opportunity to acquaint himself with the second letter. Does that not mean he was given an opportunity during the interview to look at that document and that was recorded in the interview? 14 A. Well, I would point out that I am afraid I have not understood your question as put. 16 Q. Well, what I am curious about is why you say this document was produced during the interview and it does not say that it was produced before him. On page 11 that we have been looking at where you have been asked to consider this Exhibit, it does not state that it was produced before him, does it? 21 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: I think he is still looking at page 3. 22 MR. KAY: Yes. If you would like to look at page 17 of the German document. 24 A. Yes, I am looking at that now. 25 Q. It does not say it was actually produced for him to look at, does it? 27 A. I can just repeat what I said earlier on, the document was produced and Mr. Tadic did have an opportunity to acquaint himself with that document. 2 Q. How many other documents were then produced during this interview? 4 A. I already indicated that. All of the exhibits that have their own reference number were produced in the course of the interview. 7 MR. KAY: Thank you. That is all I ask. 8 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: Mr. Keegan?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 10 Q. Officer Huebel, the production of specific exhibits or documents referred to, you testified earlier is the standard procedure for German police authorities? 13 A. It is a standard procedure in Germany when reference is made to exhibits, and when there is any need to mention exhibits those exhibits are produced to the person involved and the person involved is given a chance to look at them. 17 Q. The accused had a Defence counsel present during this interview, correct? 19 A. During the three days of interviews, from the first to the last minute the German Defence counsel of Mr. Tadic was present throughout. He could follow the proceedings and he had the opportunity to make any objections he might have cared to. 23 Q. This first document which the Defence counsel asked you about which was attached as an annex, that was in fact separate, if you will, from the actual interview itself? 26 A. That was a separate matter because in those handwritten notes Mr. Tadic had made some statements about himself and about his activities, and that is why that was referred to in the part entitled "About the Individual". 2 Q. In the comment that follows there are additions or corrections, if you will, that the accused himself wanted to make for the record? 5 A. What was entered into further on is a fuller understanding of the elements relating to the individual Mr. Tadic. 7 MR. KEEGAN: Thank you. Nothing further, your Honour. 8 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: Mr. Kay? 9 MR. KAY: Thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 11 Q. You have just told us that Mr. Tadic was interviewed over three days, is that right? 13 A. That is right, Mr. Tadic was questioned over a three-day period. 14 Q. How many pages of interview do we have for that questioning during the period of three days? 16 A. Now I have here the front page 1 to 31 and that is the full record, the full transcript of the interview of Mr. Tadic. 18 Q. When you refer to this passage of the interview at page 11, page 17 of your document, it does not say that Mr. Tadic looked at the document, does it? 21 A. I can just reiterate what I have already said and repeat that Mr. Tadic did see that document. It was produced. 23 Q. Well, there is a difference between a document being produced and a document being looked at. You understand that difference, do you? 26 A. Mr. Tadic was shown this document and he had the opportunity to examine it more closely and read what it said. 28 Q. So when you say he had the opportunity to examine it more closely and see what it said, that does not mean that he did look at it more closely? 3 A. We gave him the opportunity to look at the document, to read it, and Mr. Tadic did see the document and Mr. Tadic could read the document. He was granted the time and the possibility to do so. 6 Q. His reply was he knew nothing about it and he did not receive any weapons or any ammunition from the staff of the Territorial Defence, is that right? 9 A. That is also what we put in the record. 10 MR. KAY: Thank you very much. 11 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: Mr. Keegan? 12 MR. KEEGAN: No nothing, your Honour. 13 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: Sir, you are permanently excused. You are free to leave, but you need to remain where you are sitting. The Judges will leave so that we can then go back into open session. So you remain where you are sitting, but you are free to go after we have left. 18 3.50 p.m. (The Court adjourned for a short time). 20 3.55 p.m. 21 MR. NIEMANN: Your Honours, the one thing remaining I think is that there was a piece of paper shown, two pieces of paper shown to Witness AA this morning and I tender those. Might they be given collectively the number 370? They are just two pieces of paper with names on them, your Honours. Might they be sealed? 26 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: Yes, they will be marked as Prosecution 370 and 371 or together? 28 MR. NIEMANN: 370A and B. 1 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: Any objection? 2 MR. KAY: No, your Honour. 3 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: They will be admitted and sealed. 4 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: Is there anything else, Mr. Niemann? 5 MR. NIEMANN: No, your Honours, that concludes the evidence of the Prosecution in rebuttal. 7 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: Mr. Wladimiroff? 8 MR. WLADIMIROFF: Thank you, your Honour. We will not call for evidence in rejoinder, your Honours. 10 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: The Chamber wants to thank counsel, of course, for the very professional way that you presented the evidence. We have scheduled closing arguments for November 25th at 10 a.m. and have reserved two days, but we are willing to go to three days to listen to you for as long as you wish. So we encourage you to take your time and present the evidence fully. It has been a long trial with a number of Exhibits and many thousands of pages of testimony. We will adjourn then until November 25th at 10 a.m. (The Court adjourned) 20 21 22 23 24 25 26 27 28
